content: Neonates represent a highly vulnerable patient group, with approximately 6% to 9% requiring admission to the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) after birth. During their NICU stay, neonates are subjected to multiple painful procedures daily. Evidence increasingly suggests that repeated exposure to painful stimuli during this critical period is associated with adverse long-term outcomes. To address this, various pain management strategies have been developed, including pharmacological and non-pharmacological approaches. This review specifically focused on non-opioid analgesics, such as non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor antagonists, which work by modulating cellular pathways to provide pain relief. While these analgesics show promise in clinical practice, there is a lack of comprehensive evidence summarizing their benefits and potential harms. The review aimed to evaluate the level of pain experienced by neonates during and after procedures, the occurrence of adverse events such as apnea, desaturation, bradycardia, and hypotension, and the effects of combining different drugs. Given the evolving nature of neonatal pain management, the goal was to provide an evidence-based overview of non-opioid analgesic options to guide clinical practice. The objective of the review was to assess the effects of non-opioid analgesics in neonates, both term and preterm, undergoing painful procedures. These effects were compared to placebo, no drug, non-pharmacological interventions, other analgesics, or different routes of administration. The search strategy included databases such as the Cochrane Library, PubMed, Embase, and two trial registries, with the last search conducted in June 2022. Reference lists of included studies were also screened for additional relevant studies. The inclusion criteria encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, and cluster-RCTs involving neonates undergoing painful procedures, comparing NSAIDs and NMDA receptor antagonists to other interventions. Standard Cochrane methods were used for data collection and analysis. The primary outcomes assessed were pain during the procedure and up to 10 minutes afterward, using validated pain scales, as well as episodes of bradycardia, apnea, and hypotension requiring medical intervention. Two RCTs involving 269 neonates from Nigeria and India were included in the review. One RCT evaluated the use of oral ketamine (10 mg/kg) versus sugar syrup (66.7% w/w at 1 mL/kg) for neonatal circumcision. The evidence regarding the effect of ketamine on pain scores during the procedure, as measured by the Neonatal Infant Pain Scale (NIPS), was highly uncertain (mean difference [MD] −0.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] −1.32 to −0.58; very low-certainty evidence). No other relevant outcomes were reported in this study. Another RCT compared intravenous ketamine to intravenous fentanyl during laser photocoagulation for retinopathy of prematurity. Neonates receiving ketamine were administered either an initial bolus dose of 0.5 mg/kg one minute before the procedure or additional intermittent bolus doses of 0.5 mg/kg every 10 minutes, up to a maximum of 2 mg/kg. Those receiving fentanyl were given either an initial dose of 2 μg/kg over five minutes, 15 minutes before the procedure, followed by a continuous infusion of 1 μg/kg/hour, or a revised regimen involving titration of 0.5 μg/kg/hour every 15 minutes, up to a maximum of 3 μg/kg/hour. The evidence was very uncertain regarding the effect of ketamine compared to fentanyl on pain scores during the procedure, as measured by the Premature Infant Pain Profile-Revised (PIPP-R) (MD 0.98, 95% CI 0.75 to 1.20; very low-certainty evidence). Similarly, the evidence was very uncertain regarding the occurrence of apnea during the procedure (risk ratio [RR] 0.31, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.18; risk difference [RD] −0.09, 95% CI −0.19 to 0.00) and hypotension requiring medical therapy (RR 5.53, 95% CI 0.27 to 112.30; RD 0.03, 95% CI −0.03 to 0.10). This study did not report pain scores up to 10 minutes after the procedure or episodes of bradycardia. No studies were identified that compared NSAIDs to placebo, no treatment, oral sweet solutions, or non-pharmacological interventions. Additionally, no studies evaluated different routes of administration for the same analgesics. Three studies were identified as awaiting classification. The authors concluded that the two small included studies, which compared ketamine to either placebo or fentanyl, provided very low-certainty evidence, making it impossible to draw definitive conclusions. The evidence regarding the effect of ketamine on pain scores during procedures, compared to placebo or fentanyl, remains highly uncertain. No evidence was found regarding the use of NSAIDs or comparisons of different routes of administration. Future research should prioritize large-scale studies evaluating non-opioid analgesics in neonates. Given the potential benefits suggested by the included studies, further investigation into ketamine is warranted. Additionally, studies on NSAIDs, which are commonly used in older infants, and comparisons of different administration routes should be prioritized.
